images.title: A tiny solved Hidato
images.purpose: Show what a finished Hidato looks like: a path of consecutive numbers through touching cells, including a diagonal step.
images.composition: One 3 by 3 square grid large in the centre of the frame with a path line drawn through the cell centres, and white space all round.
exact_structure: 1 grid of 3 rows and 3 columns of equal square cells, thin dark outlines, 9 cells in all
Cells holding 1 and 9 shaded light teal #0072B2 as the given lowest and highest numbers
1 continuous reddish purple #CC79A7 path line through the cell centres in order 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
The step from 3 to 4 (a diagonal move) drawn as a thicker green #009E73 segment, with the label 'Corners count too' beside it outside the grid
rejection: any number in a different cell from the layout given
the path skipping a number or joining cells that do not touch
a grid size other than 3 by 3
the highlighted diagonal on any step other than 3 to 4
images.takeaway: In Hidato each number touches the next one, side or corner, so the numbers form one unbroken path from lowest to highest.
images.description: A 3 by 3 Hidato grid filled 1 to 9 with a path joining consecutive numbers and the diagonal step from 3 to 4 highlighted.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text on the rules of Hidato.
images.teaching_notes: Trace the path with a finger and check every step touches the last one before trying the bigger grids.

image_decisions.why: A small solved grid shows the path rule, including diagonal moves, faster than words.
